title: When the Number Is Right and the Claim Is Wrong

steps.body:
The arithmetic can be perfect while the sentence is false. Three ways it happens:

**Reach** — the claim covers people the sample never included.
**Extrapolation** — the claim runs past the range of the data.
**Swapped conditional** — P(A | B) reported as P(B | A).

Each one is a failure of *interpretation*, not of computation.

explanationVariants: The sample was drawn from one city's commuters, so the estimate describes that group and no other.
Generalising to "all workers" invents a population that was never sampled.

widget.prompt: A random sample of commuters at one city's train station finds 61% support a fare freeze. Which claim overreaches?

options.label: "61% of all workers in the country support a fare freeze."
options.feedback: Right — the sample was random within train commuters in one city, so it can speak for them and nobody else.

options.label: "About 61% of this station's commuters support a fare freeze, ± the margin."
options.feedback: That is exactly the claim the design supports: random within the population sampled, and honest about the margin.

options.label: "Support among these commuters is plausibly between 57% and 65%."
options.feedback: A perfectly legal band, provided those numbers came from the margin of error.

options.label: "We cannot say what car drivers think from this sample."
options.feedback: True and appropriately modest — car drivers were never eligible to be picked.

steps.body: A line fitted to data from 20 to 60 minutes of study.

widget.prompt: Study time (minutes) against test score, for 20–60 minutes. Fit the best straight line — then read what it predicts at 600 minutes.
widget.successFeedback: About ŷ = 0.77x + 37 — an excellent fit across 20 to 60 minutes. Now extend it to 600 minutes and it predicts a score near 500 on a 100-point test. The model is not wrong; it is being used outside the range the data ever visited. That is extrapolation, and it is the failure this lesson is about.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Move the slope until the line runs through the middle of the points: roughly 0.77 with an intercept near 37.
widget.slopeFeedback: The tilt is off. Each extra 10 minutes buys roughly 8 points, so the slope should sit near 0.77 — not far from 0.8.
widget.offsetFeedback: The tilt looks right but the line sits too high or too low. Slide the intercept until the line passes through the middle of the points, around 37.

explanationVariants: The data run from 20 to 60 minutes. A prediction at 600 minutes is a guess dressed as arithmetic.
The relationship almost certainly bends — sleep and fatigue arrive — but the line has no way of knowing that.

widget.prompt: A line fitted to study times of 20–60 minutes predicts a score of 200 at 10 hours. What went wrong?

options.label: The prediction is far outside the range of the data, so the model has no evidence to stand on.
options.feedback: Right — and the 200 on a 100-point test is the tell. A model is only evidence about the range it was fitted to.

options.label: The line was fitted incorrectly.
options.feedback: The fit may be excellent within 20–60 minutes. The failure happens the moment it is asked about a place the data never went.

options.label: Study time does not affect scores.
options.feedback: Inside the observed range it clearly does — about 3 points per 10 minutes. The trouble is only with the leap beyond the data.

options.label: The sample was too small.
options.feedback: Even a million students studying 20–60 minutes would tell you nothing about ten-hour sessions. It is a range problem, not a size problem.

steps.body:
The third failure is the reversal you met in probability.

"95% of people with the disease test positive" is P(positive | disease).
"95% of positive tests mean disease" is P(disease | positive).

When the disease is rare, these two numbers are wildly different — and the second one is usually the false claim in the headline.

explanationVariants: Of 10,000 people, 100 have the disease and 95 of them test positive. Of the 9,900 healthy people, 5% — 495 — also test positive. So of 590 positives, only 95 truly have it: about 16%.
A 95% accurate test on a 1-in-100 disease gives mostly false positives, because the healthy group is a hundred times larger.

widget.prompt: A disease affects 1% of people. A test catches 95% of cases and wrongly flags 5% of healthy people. Out of 10,000 people, how many POSITIVE results are there in total?

numericErrors.feedback: That counts only the true positives (95% of the 100 who are ill). The healthy group also produces positives — 5% of 9,900 is 495 more.
That is roughly the false positives alone (5% of 9,900 = 495). The 95 true positives belong in the total as well.
That is the number of people who actually have the disease, not the number who test positive.

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.
widget.fallbackFeedback: 95 true positives + 495 false positives = 590 positive results.
widget.successFeedback: 95 true positives + 495 false positives = 590 positive results.

hints: You have 590 positive results in total. How many of those people actually have the disease?
Only the 95 true positives are genuinely ill. The other 495 are healthy people the test flagged wrongly.
So compute 95/590 and express it as a percentage, rounded to a whole number.
explanationVariants: P(disease | positive) = 95/590 ≈ 16%. The headline's "95% accurate" was P(positive | disease) — a completely different number.
The healthy group is 99 times larger, so even a small false-positive RATE produces a large false-positive COUNT that swamps the true cases.

widget.prompt: Of those 590 positive results, what percentage of people actually have the disease? (whole number)

numericErrors.feedback: That is the test's catch rate, P(positive | disease). You are being asked the reverse: P(disease | positive), which divides the 95 true positives by all 590 positives.
That is the healthy fraction of the population, not a conditional on a positive test.
That is the false-positive rate for healthy people. The question asks what share of POSITIVES are genuinely ill: 95/590.

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.

takeaways: A claim may not reach beyond the population that was actually sampled.
A model is evidence only inside the range of its data — extrapolation is assumption, not inference.
"95% accurate" is P(positive | disease). For a rare disease, P(disease | positive) can be tiny.
steps.teaser: Last lesson: everything at once, on claims from the wild.

concept.body: Ask two questions of any conclusion. **Who does it speak for?** Only the people who could have been sampled. **Where does it apply?** Only inside the range of the data. A conclusion that leaves either boundary is no longer supported by the study.

explanationVariants: The sample came from one hospital's patients, so the estimate speaks for that group.
Extending it to the general public would include people who had no chance of being sampled.

widget.prompt: A random sample of one hospital's patients finds 30% have high blood pressure. Which claim is supported?

options.label: About 30% of that hospital's patients have high blood pressure.
options.feedback: Right — random within the population sampled, and it speaks for that population only.

options.label: About 30% of the country has high blood pressure.
options.feedback: Hospital patients are a sicker group than the country as a whole, and nobody outside the hospital could have been sampled.
